rationale: Both verses open with the identical imperative הָג֣וֹ (oshb:Prov.25.4) / הָג֣וֹ (oshb:Prov.25.5) ("remove"), a skeleton token that occurs nowhere else in this part. v4 states the metallurgical figure (remove dross from silver, material emerges for the refiner); v5 supplies the referent it illustrates (remove the wicked from before the king, and his throne is established in righteousness). The figure-then-referent pairing, anchored by the shared verse-initial imperative, argues the two as one unit.
rejected_alternative: Reading 25:4 alone as a closed metallurgical proverb was rejected: without v5 the figure has no stated referent, and the repeated verse-initial imperative signals a deliberate figure/referent pair rather than two unrelated sayings.

rationale: The verse pairs a positive imperative (argue your own case directly with your neighbor, רֵעֶ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.25.9)) with a negative one (do not disclose another's confidence); both halves are complete as advice without requiring the next verse's warning. 25:10's warning clause reads naturally as the consequence of the second half of this verse, but the dependency is a warning appended after an already-complete instruction rather than a syntactic requirement for v9 to parse. The verse's closing word רֵעֶ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.25.9) recurs at the left seam: 25:8 closes with the same word, רֵעֶֽךָ (oshb:Prov.25.8), and both verses carry the root ר-י-ב (לָרִ֗ב in 25:8, "to strive"; רִ֣יב in 25:9, "argue your case"), disclosed as left-seam texture, not a boundary driver.
rejected_alternative: Merging with 25:10 was rejected: v9's imperative pair is a complete instruction on its own, and the warning clause of v10 functions as an added caution rather than an obligatory completion (contrast the true syntactic split at 26:18-19).
observed_substrate_signals: web:Prov.25.9 two coordinated imperatives complete the verse's advice
device_notes: Synonymous-to-synthetic parallelism: direct engagement with the neighbor set against the prohibition on disclosing a secret.

rationale: Both verses share the exact skeleton token זָ֭הָב (oshb:Prov.25.11) / זָ֭הָב (oshb:Prov.25.12) ("gold"), which recurs at only one other site in this part (27:21), and both use the same construction: a valuable ornament named without a comparison particle, equated directly with a quality of speech (a fitly-spoken word; a wise reprover to an obedient ear). The twin gold-ornament equations, back to back and exactly repeated -- their adjacency and exact repetition, not part-wide exclusivity, is what argues clustering -- argue for one row.
rejected_alternative: Reading the two verses independently was rejected given the bounded exact-token repetition and the shared no-particle equation construction distinctive to this adjacent pair.

rationale: The two verses repeat the closing phrase כְּ֭סִיל כְּאִוַּלְתּ֑וֹ (oshb:Prov.26.4) / כְ֭סִיל כְּאִוַּלְתּ֑וֹ (oshb:Prov.26.5) ("a fool according to his folly") -- identical but for a dagesh point on the kesil token -- while flatly reversing the governing imperative -- תַּ֣עַן (oshb:Prov.26.4) ("do not answer", with the preceding אל) in v4 against עֲנֵ֣ה (oshb:Prov.26.5) ("answer") in v5 -- the book's own documented deliberate-contradiction pair, cited here by the contradiction itself.

A harmonizing reading that resolves the contradiction into a single unproblematic rule was also rejected, since the verses are kept grammatically opposite rather than merged into one instruction.

rationale: v18 gives just the protasis of a comparison -- "like a madman who shoots torches, arrows, and death" -- lacking a finite predicate for a human referent; the apodosis completing the sentence is supplied in v19, opening כֵּֽן אִ֭ישׁ (oshb:Prov.26.19) ("so is the man") who deceives his neighbor and calls it a joke. Unlike the 5 other comparative similes in this part, which each complete within one verse (26:1, 26:2, 26:8, 27:8, 27:19), this is the one instance where the comparison particle and its resolving apodosis sit in different verses: one syntactically continuous sentence spanning the verse seam, not two sayings joined by a shared theme.
rejected_alternative: Reading 26:18 as its own complete simile was rejected: its participial protasis lacks a finite predicate for a human referent without v19's apodosis clause, and the 5 other comparative similes in this part (26:1, 26:2, 26:8, 27:8, 27:19) each complete within one verse. Reading the pair as a proverb_cluster of two sayings was also rejected: there are no multiple independent sayings here to cohere, just one sentence split by the verse boundary.

rationale: v23 opens with an infinitive-absolute-plus-cognate-imperfect emphatic assertion, יָדֹ֣עַ תֵּ֭דַע (oshb:Prov.27.23) ("you shall surely know"), paired with one true Qal 2ms imperative, שִׁ֥ית לִ֝בְּךָ֗ (oshb:Prov.27.23) ("set your heart"), both addressed to the state of the flocks and herds; v24 supplies the motive clause כִּ֤י לֹ֣א לְעוֹלָ֣ם חֹ֑סֶן (oshb:Prov.27.24) ("for riches are not forever"; v24 also carries an unrelated ketiv/qere note later in the verse, on its generation-to-generation phrase), explaining why ongoing attention is needed; v25 describes the grass cycle that sustains the flocks named in v23 (a third-person description bridging command and result); v26-27 return to the same 2ms addressee of v23 to list what the flocks yield -- clothing, a field's price, milk for food and household and servants. The assertion-imperative-motive-support-result chain, framed by one consistent addressee, argues the five verses as one instruction rather than five independent sayings.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the five verses into single-verse rows was rejected because v24's motive clause depends on v23's command and v25's grass cycle supplies the ecological premise for v26-27's yield list, with the 2ms addressee bracketing the whole. Splitting at v25 alone (isolating the descriptive middle verse) was also considered and rejected, since v25's grass-and-hay cycle is the stated precondition for the very flocks whose products are listed in v26-27, not an independent nature saying.
